claims.text: Engineered multilayer interfaces in high-entropy-alloy protective coatings act as barriers to dislocation motion and thereby suppress creep.
Thinner layer spacing enhances dislocation trapping and recombination at interfaces relative to thicker-layer or homogeneous coatings.
The coatings have well-defined compositional gradients and layer architecture in their as-deposited or service-ready state.
Systematically varying layer thickness and testing under constant load at elevated temperature provides a controlled way to compare creep behavior.
High-temperature nano-indentation can be used to measure time-dependent deformation in high-entropy alloys.
The multilayer interfaces serve as both dislocation barriers and dislocation-trapping sites.
Under sustained load at elevated temperature, dislocations can nucleate and move as part of the creep response.
Compositional and structural discontinuities at multilayer interfaces impede dislocation motion.
Impeded dislocation motion at the interfaces causes dislocation pile-ups and enhanced recovery.
Dislocation-interface interactions retard time-dependent plastic deformation.
Optimized, especially thinner, layer spacing will produce lower creep displacement rates than homogeneous or thicker-layer coatings.
Optimized, especially thinner, layer spacing will produce higher creep activation energies than homogeneous or thicker-layer coatings.
Homogeneous or single-layer high-entropy-alloy coatings are expected to have higher creep deformation rates than multilayer coatings.
The proposed interface-barrier mechanism is applicable primarily where dislocation-mediated creep dominates.
Stress and temperature can change the dominant creep mechanism, so alternative mechanisms may prevail outside the proposed regime.
The interface-barrier mechanism is expected to remain effective below the coating's onset of thermal degradation.
The quantitative relationship between layer thickness and barrier strength, including the optimal layer spacing, is unknown.

The hypothesis would be falsified if multilayer coatings show neither significantly lower creep rates or higher activation energies nor pronounced dislocation-interface interactions relative to the homogeneous control.
